title: Bone Marrow Biopsy
subject: Pathology
summary: Bone marrow biopsy obtains a core of marrow for microscopic evaluation, confirming or excluding hematologic disorders. In low‑resource settings it guides treatment when peripheral tests are limited.

sections.p: A bone marrow biopsy is a percutaneous core‑needle sampling of the posterior iliac crest (or sternum) examined histologically to assess cellularity, lineage maturation and infiltrative disease.
b: Gold‑standard for unexplained pancytopenia, suspected leukaemia, myeloproliferative neoplasms and marrow failure.
Provides material for morphology, immunophenotyping and cytogenetics.

sections.p: Marrow findings are graded by cellularity (% of hematopoietic cells) and by disease‑specific criteria (e.g., WHO classification for leukaemia, IPSS for myelodysplasia).
b: Hypocellular <30 % → severe aplastic anaemia.
Hypercellular >80 % with blasts >20 % → acute leukaemia.

sections.p: In East African hospitals the common indications for biopsy are:
b: Aplastic anaemia (benzene exposure, viral hepatitis, HIV).
Acute leukaemia (often secondary to malaria‑induced marrow stress).
Myelodysplastic syndrome (rare, but increasing with HIV therapy).
Infection‑related marrow suppression (TB, disseminated fungal disease).
Hemoglobinopathies (sickle cell crisis with aplastic episodes).

sections.p: Patients usually present with cytopenia‑related symptoms: fatigue, infections, bleeding, or unexplained fever. Physical exam may show pallor, petechiae, or splenomegaly.
b: Pancytopenia → consider aplastic anaemia, infiltration or marrow failure.
Isolated neutropenia → possible HIV or TB marrow involvement.

sections.p: Bone marrow biopsy is integrated with bedside labs and imaging.

t.b: Is there cytopenia? → Guides need for marrow sampling; if unavailable, treat presumptively for infection.
Low retic with anaemia → points to production problem; high retic suggests peripheral loss.
Cellularity, lineage maturation, blasts, iron stores → defines disease; if core unavailable, rely on aspirate morphology.
Immunophenotype of blasts → distinguishes leukaemia subtypes; if flow unavailable, use morphology and clinical picture.
Detect translocations, prognostic lesions → informs therapy; if not available, treat based on WHO morphological category.

t.a: Serology for HIV, hepatitis B/C, TB (Quantiferon)
t.b: Identify infectious contributors to marrow suppression → treat underlying infection.

sections.p: Complications are rare but can be serious.
b: Severe pain or expanding hematoma at puncture site → consider arterial injury.
Persistent fever after biopsy → rule out infection.
Pathological fracture in osteolytic disease.

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first; supportive care follows.
b: Aplastic anaemia: immunosuppression (antithymocyte globulin, cyclosporine) when donor marrow unavailable; avoid high‑dose steroids alone.
Acute leukaemia: induction chemotherapy (anthracycline + cytarabine) – avoid agents that cause excessive myelosuppression if marrow already hypocellular.
Infection‑related suppression: appropriate antimicrobials (e.g., rifampicin for TB, antiretrovirals for HIV).
Supportive: transfuse packed RBCs for symptomatic anaemia, platelets for bleeding, prophylactic antibiotics for neutropenia.

sections.p: Repeat marrow after 4–6 weeks if initial biopsy was nondiagnostic or after therapy to assess response.
b: Monitor blood counts weekly during treatment.
Vaccinate against hepatitis B and pneumococcus to reduce marrow‑injuring infections.
Avoid known marrow toxins (benzene, certain herbal remedies).
Peripheral blood smear showing leukaemic cells – marrow needed to confirm infiltration.
Splenomegaly‑related cytopenia – imaging helps differentiate sequestration from marrow failure.
A ‘dry tap’ may occur in myelofibrosis; a normal aspirate does not exclude fibrosis – core biopsy is essential.
Iron staining can be falsely high in chronic inflammation; correlate with serum ferritin.

whenToSeekHelp: Bleeding that does not stop with pressure
Rapidly rising blasts on peripheral smear

faq.q: Why is a core biopsy preferred over aspirate alone?
faq.a: Core provides architecture, cellularity and fibrosis assessment, which aspirate cannot.

faq.q: Can a bone‑marrow biopsy be done without anaesthesia?
faq.a: Local lidocaine is standard; pain control improves sample quality.

faq.q: What if the laboratory cannot perform flow cytometry?
faq.a: Rely on morphology, clinical context and treat empirically for the most likely disease.

exam: A 25‑year‑old with HIV presents with pancytopenia – what is your next diagnostic step and why? — Perform bone‑marrow biopsy to differentiate HIV‑related suppression from opportunistic infiltration.
How does a myeloid‑erythroid ratio of 1:4 guide your diagnosis? — Indicates erythroid hyperplasia, typical of haemolysis or ineffective erythropoiesis, not aplastic anaemia.
What red‑flag finding on biopsy would change management from supportive to urgent chemotherapy? — Presence of >20 % blasts confirming acute leukaemia.
If the biopsy is ‘dry tap’, what is the most likely underlying pathology and next step? — Suggests myelofibrosis; obtain a trephine core or consider imaging for marrow fibrosis.

Why is antithymocyte globulin preferred over high‑dose steroids in aplastic anaemia? — ATG targets immune‑mediated marrow destruction with better remission rates; steroids lack efficacy and increase infection risk.
In a patient with suspected malaria‑induced marrow suppression, why might a biopsy still be indicated? — To exclude concurrent leukaemia or severe aplasia that would require different therapy.
What infection should be screened for before starting immunosuppression for aplastic anaemia? — Hepatitis B and C, because reactivation can be fatal under immunosuppression.

How would you manage a patient with a biopsy showing hypercellular marrow but normal peripheral counts? — Monitor for early myeloproliferative disease; repeat counts and consider molecular testing if available.
